paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: the LORD of Hosts is over everything people build their lives on. Tyre was "the merchant of the nations," with ships, harbors and princes for traders (Isaiah 23:3, 8). Then Isaiah says the LORD of Hosts planned it, "to defile all its glorious beauty, to disgrace all the renowned of the earth" (Isaiah 23:9). Whatever the world calls glorious, it all stands under Him.

Now look at the second half, because this is where it gets good. Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, and I know a little something about being forgotten, since I spent years in the back of a junk drawer (Isaiah 23:15). But Isaiah says "the LORD will restore Tyre" (Isaiah 23:17). Forgotten is not the last word when He's the One writing the ending.

And the last verse has a turn that makes me want to dance on my gold base. Tyre's profits "will be set apart to the LORD," and they go to those who live before Him, "for abundant food and fine clothing" (Isaiah 23:18). So the wealth that once puffed up a city ends up taking care of His people. Baker, here's what that means for you: hold your success, your plans and your stuff loosely, because the LORD owns it all and He knows how to use it well.
